utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to you, as well, Witness DST-043. And I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony is still binding, that is, that you shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jordash, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I hope you are feeling better today and we can proceed clearly and concisely, and I'll try to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, on the screen 1D4920.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D325, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go through this systematically, Mr. Witness. Firstly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you had forgotten to tell that it was under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I want you to look first of all at the stamp at the left-hand corner and the stamp at the right-hand bottom corner. What is that stamp, do you recognise it? Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a stamp of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina. It's a stamp that was used at the SUP in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you recall who stamped this document?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document was stamped by Petojevic, Stevo, and Radovan Vrzina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who is Petojevic, Stevo?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a man who worked at the treasury in common affairs in the SUP in Knin and also in the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There is a signature in the left-hand bottom of the document. Whose signature is that, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the signature of Stevo Petojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you say he was a man who worked at the treasury in the common affairs. What was the common affairs of the treasury? What did it do?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This service did the payments, daily allowances, various costs that resulted from the functioning of the public security station and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's just break that down. Payments, what kind of payments?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The payments of salaries, of daily allowances, and other daily minor or major costs. It was a finance service and it was a part of the common services. They were employees of the finance section.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What kind of personnel received salaries through this route?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the employees received salaries this way, all those employed in the SUP of the SAO Krajina in the Knin Security Station. Every station had separate cashiers and separate services.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The Knin Security Station, is that different or the same as the police station?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same thing. The public security station or the police station in Knin was the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did the Knin Public Security Station or the Police Station have any supervisory role in relation to the other public security stations in the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say every station had separate cashiers and separate services, what exactly do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that each SUP or each police station in Knin, Benkovac, Gradacac, they had their own cashier and they had a separate log-book for daily allowances, for daily payments made, or payments received for purchasing office materials or other materials. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the various police stations, was there a sharing of funds or did they organise their funds separately according to each police station?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You mentioned Radovan Drzina as another person who operated the stamp. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a cashier and he made payments, he received payments, and he worked until late 1995 as a cashier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, returning to the document on the screen, whose writing is that? Who wrote the receipt?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where was it written?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was written in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It says in the document that the amount received from you was "brought from Munchen on the name," what does that mean? "Cupkovic, Petar, brought from Munchen on the name"; do you know what that means? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What does it mean "on the name"? "Brought from Munchen on the name"?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From. Basically it would mean from Slobodan Milunovic and Luka Lalic. On the name means from, from Slobodan Milunovic and Luka Lalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was Slobodan and Lalic, who were they?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lalic was a Serb from Krajina. He took this block of receipts. And Slobodan Milunovic was a priest in Munich.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What do you mean that Lalic was a Serb -- sorry, let me start that again. Where did Lalic live at the time this receipt was formed or written?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lalic lived in Germany at the time that this receipt was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "he took this block of receipts"?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was issued this block of receipts because when he was issued this, he also received some thank-you notes so that he could give those to the people who donate money. And he visited the area of Knin. He came to Knin from Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when was he issued a block of receipts?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the date exactly, but I believe it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who issued him the block of receipts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, would it assist you if you look at the transcript of yesterday: "I took a booklet of receipts, each of which had three copies. I handed them over to Luka Lalic." Well, if you want to know it again, then of course feel free to ask, but ... and that was in the course of 1991, as the witness said yesterday. That was your previous question. And then he said that there was a number of thank-you notes, that was part of his answer today again in response to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 12970 in the middle of the page. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that this was receipt number 48. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I see whether I understand the testimony of the witness. Is it true that you gave a booklet of receipts to Mr. Lalic, that he collected the money in Germany, that he issued receipts for those who donated money, and that at the end the total amount of money was fetched from Germany, was brought to Knin, and that the total amount was 9.970, and that upon delivery of the money in Knin that receipt number 48 was delivered; is that what you told us yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in relation to receipts 1 to 47, are you able to comment on those receipts?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't comment on that. I don't know what amounts were registered on them, but I do know that some payments were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And where did the payments come from? From the same source?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from the same source. Payments were made by various other sources. I don't know who but it wasn't from this source. Only this one receipt arrived from that source. But there were various people who collected money. There were some people who came and donated money voluntarily. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Mr. Lalic then collect money from other countries or other locations in Germany?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, my fault. Where was Mr. Lalic collecting money from which gave rise to the issuance of these receipts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "these receipts," Mr. Jordash? Not the one on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, you asked the witness: "Did Mr. Lalic then collect money from other countries or other locations?" The answer was: "No." So, therefore, "Where was Mr. Lalic collecting from money from which gave rise to the issuance of these receipts," 1 to 47 you're referring to, there's an implicit suggestion that this was money delivered by Mr. Lalic; whereas if we carefully listen to the witness, we understand that that may not have been the case. So, therefore, your question implies a -- you assume something in your question which, as far as I understand the witness says, that's not how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lalic has the receipts. I'm trying to move from that point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have -- are you aware that we have two kind of receipts? The one is the receipts Mr. Lalic gives to those who are donating money, and the other receipt is as is receipt number 48, is the receipt issued by -- in Knin for receiving the money which was collected in Germany. So we have a series of receipts in Germany given by Mr. Lalic - and I see the witness is nodding yes - to those who donated money. And then we have the receipts issued in Knin for those who brought money in Knin, including, as number 48, a total amount of 9.970 Deutschmarks collected in Germany. So these receipts is -- there are two series of receipts: the booklet of receipts Mr. Lalic took to Germany in order to give it to those who donated money, and the receipt received upon delivery of the total amount of money collected in Germany to Mr. Lalic when he brought that money in Knin. So these receipts is confusing and -- but from your answer I gained the impression that we have a totally different understanding of what the answers of the witness tell us. And if the witness disagrees with the way in which I explained it, I'd like to hear that now. But I saw you nodding yes, Witness DST-043; does that mean that I have understood your testimony well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood my testimony fully well, and if I may explain just one thing. It's correct that there were two kinds of receipts, one booklet was issued to me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I issued one to Luka Lalic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I received one from Jovo Dmitrovic or from Martic, I'm not sure who it was, I believe it was Jovo Dmitrovic. And Luka Lalic had nothing to do with this receipt. He handed over the money to me in Germany. He didn't travel to Knin. I brought the money and I received another receipt confirming that I handed the money over. And the booklet of receipts he had, he issued me one proving that he gave me the money, and I just transported it. And then when I handed over the money, I was given a receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, as far as the receipts number 1 to 47 are concerned, I think you testified that you have no details about those. Is there any reason to believe that it has got to do anything with the collection of money in Germany by Mr. Lalic, or would it be donations from who knows where but not necessarily through Mr. Lalic from Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. As for receipts 1 to 47, there were donations from Novi Sad, from Banja Luka, from various individuals, whoever came to the cash desk of the SUP or of the police station or the SJB in Knin and offered to donate money to the police was issued a receipt such as this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know how often in this period of time, July, August, around the middle of 1991, that individuals or groups of individuals were making such donations?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that very often people who were unknown to me came, and then I later heard from the cashier Radovan Vrzina or from Jovo Dmitrovic or from Nikola Rastovic that these people came and donated money. I didn't inquire about these people but we knew about the fact that money had come from donations based on the payments made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, since we're moving on to a different document, the Prosecution would just request that D325 be inventoried with the Registry. The Defence is in possession of the actual receipt and we actually ask that the item be -- remain here with the Registry as a physical object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have a copy uploaded into e-court and the original is here, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was able to see it on Sunday myself. It was produced. So if we could actually have the physical receipt inventoried with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that's on the record, that the copy will be here and will stay with the Registry. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Registry currently don't have the copy in its possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I take it that you then receive it from Mr. Jordash. If you don't receive it within the next 24 hours, please report to the Chamber. Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have 1D4921, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you just explain how this came into being and in your possession, please.

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document written in my own hand during a hand-over of these various items, in order that there be avoided any manipulations or innuendo about the whereabouts of the items concerned, this was the usual practice of putting it on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know what the -- let me start that again. Do you know who received the items and what were the items -- what was going to happen to the items? What did happen to the items?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those -- or the individuals who were supposed to be given these items, I don't know their names, but the items listed here - flour, lard, wheat, corn, et cetera - were intended for the members of the reserve police force and perhaps even some who were members of the active police force but were in some way in a vulnerable position. They were needy and had not been paid their full due salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how do you know that these items were for these personnel?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because we discussed it. We tried to find ways and means to assist these people. Furthermore, there were some items in this batch which we weren't sure what their life was because the wheat that had been donated had already been infested and needed consumption -- needed to be consumed immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. You say: "We tried to find ways and means to assist these people." Who tried to find ways and means?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic, Babic, Dmitrovic, Zelenbaba. All of us knew that the situation was very hard and that people were needy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this as an exhibit, please, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection based on the testimony of the witness. We also ask that this document remain in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, any objection to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection to it remaining in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D328, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D328 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have 1D4922, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What is this and how did it come into your possession, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a sheet of paper which is in fact a receipt confirming that I gave 3.000 dinars to Martic on the 9th of September, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why did you give Martic the money?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave it to Martic because he needed it. He didn't have the funds necessary for his basic needs. In that period of time, Martic had increased expenses because he received individuals coming from far and wide to see him and he had to have the money to serve them with coffee and drinks. He was renting a flat and had two children but was left without any means because he wasn't receiving any salary. I came up to him one day and said, Mile, do you have any money? And he said, I don't. Do you want me to bring you some? And he said, Well, please do, I'll sign a receipt against it and return it to you. And that was how I came to give him 3.000 dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to the second page of this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And could you just comment on this? Can you recall this receipt and the circumstances which gave rise to it?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This receipt is very similar to the one before. I think that this took place in Golubic. Martic was supposed to move somewhere else together with his staff and had increased expenses for cigarettes, food, and his personal needs, so I gave him the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you make the same -- or could you comment, please, on the first entry; the 31st of August, 1990, giving Martic 4.000 dinars. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall doing this and I am certain that I handed over all the various sums as recorded here to Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know why Martic was so in need of this money?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He needed the money for day-to-day costs which were higher in that period for food, cigarettes, expendable material, fuel. This because he did not have any clout at the time or power to obtain funds from the treasury of the SUP in Knin or the police station in Knin. At the time of these events, the chief of police and secretary of the station was Slobodan Vujko, who did not have the authority to finance insurgency or to give Martic any money.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if Martic's financial situation changed in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were cases such as this one in 1991, but we did not draw up any receipts. His situation did not change in 1991 for the better, save for the fact that he was appointed to a higher position and was never again in a situation where he would be completely penniless, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to recall any specific cases such as this one in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember countless times in 1991 giving Martic not just money but also cigarettes or anything else he needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if others other than yourself gave Martic such items in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a few times when I inquired of him if he needed anything and if he had any money, he would tell me, Thank you, I don't need any now, I was given some by such and such a person. Of course, I can't remember their names now. It's been a long time. On this particular receipt you can see that I added in my own hand: plus 1.000 dinars given by Janko Cvjetan from his own pocket. I can't recall specifically what the circumstances were, but perhaps I spoke to Janko Cvjetan complaining of the hardship and he offered to give some of his money. And I think that this money was given to Martic at the same time on this same occasion. Likewise, at the bottom of this sheet of paper that I happen to have in my pocket, it's my handwriting, it is written: plus on the 4th of September, 1990, in Restaurant Balkan. This was an occasion when Martic was hosting a group of visitors and didn't have any money, so I gave him some. I didn't ask him to sign against the receipt, but he always insisted that I should put it on paper. Also I didn't want to have any problems with my wife and my family about the money seeming to disappear. I used this receipt more to justify myself before my family than before anyone else, including this Tribunal. Also, what is added in -- at the bottom is: Dragan Batas, in Strmica, at his own home. He received 2.000 from me. After he fell out with Martic [as interpreted], Dragan Batas became Jovan Raskovic's driver and he didn't have any money to speak of and he didn't have money to buy a proper suit, and I did want him to appear a decent man when driving Raskovic around.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: After he fell out with Milan Babic, not Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And may I ask where you received your money from to give to Martic and others?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before the war broke out, I was very well off. I had a flat, a family house, a car, and land. I sold some of the plots of land. I received a salary, as did my wife and my mom. We sold off some of the land and most people were aware of this. My brothers were also rich. We helped each other out. They knew we had money.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, finally, you say at paragraph 69 of your statement that you've never met Jovica Stanisic or Franko Simatovic but you only know them through the media. And you say Jovica Stanisic did not have any role in the politics of the Krajina. Could I just ask you to explain why you decided to give evidence for the Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any specific motives that would have prompted me to be the Defence witness for Jovica Stanisic or Franko Simatovic. My main motive for becoming Mr. Stanisic's witness is to help establish the truth before this Tribunal. If this modest knowledge that I have can be of assistance to the Defence of Mr. Stanisic to clear him of this legacy, as it were, that was imposed on him and to help the Trial Chamber arrive at the truth, that is why I'm doing it. Mr. Stanisic is not a person that I owe anything to him. Reading about him, about the events in 1995, and the effort he put in to have French pilots and other soldiers in Republika Srpska freed and released prompted me to give this small contribution of mine to clear him of the charges against him. Also I'm the sort of person who feels keenly other people's suffering, and this humanitarian gesture that Mr. Jovica Stanisic made in 1995 prompted me to become his witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in relation to Mr. Babic, do you know whether he was a healthy man at the time you knew him, mentally, physically?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a medical expert, but it did seem to me that occasionally he had tremors, especially his leg. He would often go to the toilet and stay longer in front of the mirror, and from time to time he would take certain pills I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about, since I'm not a physician. It would also happen that where an arrangement has been made or an agreement reached, he would react in an unexpected manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I've got nothing further. Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to cross-examine the witness, I have one question for you. You said you want to assist this Chamber to establish the truth, and at the same time you say you want to clear Mr. Stanisic from any allegations made against him. Now, is that the same for you? Do you say the truth is that he is not guilty; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour, this is my position: Let every person answer for one's own actions. I think it would be ideal if all those who were guilty were -- would be held to account, because all the criminals in the former Yugoslavia have a name to their face. The ordinary citizens, those of us who are merely looking on while you are trying cases here, think along these lines: Where are those, in which armchairs are they lingering, those who are responsible for the difficult position in which their people are right now? I don't think that anyone is innocent or guilty until this is established by the competent organs. Yesterday you mentioned, I believe, if I remember that some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll read part of your answer. You read about him and about the story with the French pilots and: "This prompted me to give this small contribution of mine to clear him of the charges against him." That sounds as if you expect that your testimony is such that it would clear Mr. Stanisic of the charges brought against him. Or did I not understand your testimony accurately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mean to say that my testimony would clear him of the charges, but I did believe that my contribution, in the form of my testimony, would be to help establish the facts related to the events during that period in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I don't know even now what the indictment says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just deal with some three exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just take this opportunity. The Defence hasn't tendered 1D4922 but as of right now we would have an objection as to the reliability and authenticity of it regarding the signatures, so before Mr. Jordash sat down, I just wanted to make that aware to him in case he wanted to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You can include that then, perhaps. Mr. Weber is anticipating perhaps what you had on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I was going to tender 1D4922.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you tell us anything about reliability and authenticity. And just to remind me that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's the receipts of money to Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's the diesel receipt that the witness testified about yesterday or the diesel receipts, the three diesel receipts. So it's two -- three receipts of money to Martic and Dragan Batas and two gasoline -- sorry, three gasoline receipts. And finally, a receipt relating to a book and stationery store in Knin. And in our submission the witness has testified at length about these receipts and if my learned friend wants to cross-examine him on that issue, that's entirely a matter for him, otherwise we submit the threshold has clearly been crossed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on page 18, lines 4 through 6, I objected on a very particular basis, the signatures. I don't know if the witness has provided any testimony as to whose signatures are on these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is about the receipts, the fuel receipts, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's hardly any -- there's a kind of a -- not really a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would be contesting that these are the signatures of Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. The fuel receipts, I don't think that they were supposed to have been signed by Mr. Martic. Mr. Martic was not at the fuel station to -- then apparently what you are focusing on, Mr. -- what else do we have? We have the -- the hand-written -- the 9th of September, 3.000 dinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the second one is the 17th of August, 1990, 10.000 dinar. And then a series of notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- dated the 31st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, dated the 31st of August. And later, further down, it's the 4th of September, 1990. And some of them are without any signature at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The -- there's three signatures in total. One for the -- in relation to who we say is Martic. 9th of September, 1990; 17th of August, 1990; and then the top entry of the third document, 31st of August, 1990, received by and signed by Martic. And then the three entries on the 31st -- sorry, the three entries on that third document relating to Janko Cvjetan, the Balkan Restaurant, and Dragan Batas are not signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you contest, Mr. Weber, that the two separate hand-written receipts and the top of the 31st of August, 1990, piece of paper, that is the handwriting, the signature, put there by Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. It might have been signed for him, but we are asking for testimony to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I can deal with that briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be better that I give an opportunity to Mr. Jordash to specifically address this issue with the witness and see what comes out. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D4922 page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Whose signature is that, Mr. Witness? Or do you recognise it --

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is Martic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you present or not when it was signed?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he signed it or some of his men signed it, I think he signed it. As for whether I was present, I was present when I gave him the money. But we didn't write up the receipt at that very moment. We might have written it up later on, but I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise any -- either of those signatures?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them is my signature. And as for Martic's signature, I didn't see it for many years but I assert here that I did give him this money. I really don't recall the details about him signing the receipt, but I assert here under full responsibility that I gave him the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the third page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to the 31st of August, 1990, receipt, do you recognise either signature?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them is my signature and the one on the left I think may not be Martic's. It's in Latin script. Maybe I needed to justify at home where the money was. I told you before, I didn't request that he signed for me. He insisted on signing. And underneath what it says, Janko Cvjetan gave the money, this was just a note, nobody signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's just stay with the signature a moment. You said -- you said the one on the left may not be Martic's. Do you have any idea whose it might be?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall others other than Martic signing such receipts? Who might it have been?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For him personally I can't recall. Nobody signed for him. But it could be that it was one of these people or people who were close to him so that I could justify the absence of the money at home. And so that I wouldn't humiliate him to sign for each and every one of them, it might be that somebody else signed for him. It might be his signature. I'm just not sure. And as far as I know, nobody signed on his behalf. But I do know, and I'm saying the same thing I said about the previous receipt, on my honour I claim that I gave him the money and that what it says here is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that whereas you positively repeat your testimony that you gave him the money, that for neither of the three possible signatures of Mr. Martic that you can be sure that it was him who signed either on the two separate receipts or on this third note where we find the name of Mr. Martic in Latin script?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not referring to the previous two receipts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just then interrupt you. You told us about this note but for the previous two you said you don't remember the details, they were not signed immediately after you gave the money, you do not know the circumstances under which they were signed, which I understood that you are not absolutely certain that the signatures found on the other two, that they are Mr. Martic's signatures. But if I misunderstood you, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have forgotten a long time ago what his signature looks like. I remember these receipts vaguely. There were other receipts like this signed by him personally which I intended to bring here; however, since my weekend house on Cer mountain was burgled, I lost most newspaper cuttings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand your answer to be that although there may be others where you are more certain that they were signed by Mr. Martic, that for these you do not have a clear recollection on when and under what circumstances they were signed, and that your recollection of the -- what Mr. Martic's signature looks like is such that you cannot positively confirm that this is his signature; is that a correct understanding of what you just told me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About the same. I'm sure that Martic signed receipts, but I'm not sure whether it's this signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On either of the three pieces of paper we've looked at; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the three documents, one is most certainly his signature. Perhaps two or perhaps three. One is certainly his. If you have his signature somewhere, you can compare it and you can see which of the three is his signature. But I assert under full responsibility that everything that's on these receipts is correct and that I did give him the money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said one of the three certainly is his signature. Now, can you tell us -- can you identify which of the three certainly is his signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to identify whether it's this one or the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weber, I think that on the basis of the testimony of the witness the probative value of the document is not primarily that they were signed by Mr. Martic but that they are contemporaneous notes, either with or without the signature of Mr. Martic, which were written in order to put on paper amounts of money that were given to Mr. Martic at the dates contained in these pieces of paper. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's understood. I believe the rest of the matters would be going to weight, so we withdraw our objection and to the extent that it relates to the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I also understand that your objections were limited to these three out of the seven pages of - what is it? - P -- no, 1D4922? No problem with the fuel? They are all in one batch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections from the Simatovic Defence. Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned to document 1D4922 would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would be D329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D329 is admitted under seal, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And may I then just request two documents which were part of the chart, 1D2404 and 65 ter 1896, that they be tendered but MFI'd, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, two documents known to me now by number, not by their content. 1D2404 is -- Mr. Jordash is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection to 1D2404 being marked for identification or 1896 being marked for identification. We are waiting for additional information on provenance for the Defence exhibit and we still need to discuss 1896 with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 1D2404 will be marked for identification under what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under number D330, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D330. 65 ter 1869 will be MFI'd under number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D331, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D331. Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to -- Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will also request that D329 stay in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection. The only comment I would make is that if the Prosecution wish to conduct any forensic examination of the notes, that they do so through the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, or at least I would say forensic examinations are usually best done by experts accepted by both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We will of course inform the Defence if we are going to conduct any forensic examinations and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you'll inform the Defence that you intend to have the documents examined. If there's any disagreement about who, how, under what circumstances, where, you may address the Chamber after you have had a cup of tea or a cup of coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. We would ask that the same conditions be applied as they have -- the Prosecution have applied to us with their exhibits. We're just asking for parity of treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- we can imagine what problems would arise. The next step could be, let's say, that -- but not in the Netherlands Forensic Institute or not on the beach in Scheveningen or only if you take one out of the seven pages; you can spend hours on that. You agree if one of the parties wishes the document to be examined, they contact the other party, they try to seek an agreement on how it will be done, by whom it will be done, when it will be done, on the beach, off the beach, wherever. If you do not agree, you come back to the Chamber and we'll determine the matter on the presentation of the basis of your disagreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you are not among the disagreeing parties yet. Did you wish to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's correct. Yes, I would like to cross-examine the witness. But I'm also looking at the clock, so I would like to hear your instructions about whether it's more useful to take a break now and then I would continue after the break. I would follow your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that would be the best to do, Mr. Petrovic, to take a break first. Your estimate of the time you would need, you said you would look into the matter again overnight. What is your present estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 45 minutes. Not more than 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you are on your feet where I expected Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'd hope the same. May I just apologise that we did not file a summary or didn't read out a summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all, you are supposed to present it orally before the witness starts his testimony. I do understand that it had not been prepared and that as a solution, although a bad solution, that it will be filed, but I expect the Stanisic Defence to improve its performance in this respect after the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it's important for the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there was a technical problem with the instruments used for the transcription. I think the last words I spoke was, "but I expect the Stanisic Defence to improve its performance after the recess." And then I added that it was important for the public. Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness DST-043, you are now cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. You may proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since we speak the same language, I would like to ask you to pause between my question and your answer and the other way around. So if I'm quiet and I'm not putting the next question to you, it just means that I'm waiting for the interpretation to be recorded on the transcript. I would also like you -- like to ask you to give me brief answers so that we could complete my examination as quickly as possible. Thank you in advance, witness. My first question relates to your statement, the very beginning of the statement. There is no need to have it up on the screen. You talk about the elections in the Republic of Croatia in 1990. I would like to know whether the Serbian Democratic Party of Professor Raskovic participated in the elections everywhere in Croatia, in all areas in Croatia which were populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Wherever Serbs were a majority in the Republic of Croatia, the party took part in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any areas where Serbs lived but the SDS was not organised and prepared to take part in the elections in 1990 and where they voted for other political parties?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some areas where the SDS did not put forward any candidates, and it was not prepared to take part in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that was the case, in which areas, and, if you know, for whom the Serbs mainly voted in those elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I don't recall exactly the areas where it didn't take part in the elections, but where it did take part was Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, Korenica, Gornji Lapac, Gracac, Srb, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who General Pekic was?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether he had a role in these events in late 1990 and early 1991?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not play a role apart from a large rally that was held in Petrova Gora, but I don't recall the exact date. Apart from this one rally, he did not play a major role.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement in paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please have statement D322 up on the screen without being broadcast to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that the main focus of the SDS was to fight for the institutionalisation of the position of the Serbs within the Republic of Croatia. Can you please tell us briefly what this institutionalisation of the position of the Serbs meant as you interpreted this?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The institutionalisation of the Serbs as we interpreted it at the time was what I wrote in paragraph 5, namely the political unity for all the Serbs in the Republic of Croatia, wanted to avoid assimilation, and the Serbs to have the right to their language, their culture, their freedom of expression, their media.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 7 of your statement you said that Professor Raskovic did not want the political autonomy of Serbs in Croatia. Could you explain to us, if you know, what's the difference between the political platform of Professor Raskovic and the one represented by Milan Babic? If you could describe the difference to us briefly.

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Raskovic demanded cultural autonomy, but he also said that it all depended on the moves of the Croatian authorities. We would have a policy of playing one move against another move, as you would in a game of chess. The Croatian Democratic Union, which won the elections, if they were to exhibit Ustasha-like motives in reviving the past with threats which would create insecurity and pose a threat to the people being erased from the constitution, then we would seek political autonomy, but either way at that time he said publicly that in the end it would be better if there were no Serbs in the Croatian constitution but still have them in Croatia than to have them in the constitution and not have them in Croatia. And as you know, that was his idea. And he always said that we have to seek our interests and we have to have our problems resolved in the Republic of Croatia where we live, where the graves of our ancestors are, where we have our estates, where we were born, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you described the political platform of Professor Raskovic. My question related to the difference between Raskovic's platform and that of Milan Babic. If there was a difference, could you please explain it to us?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, the concept was the same. However, as time passed after the first multi-party elections, the passion for power that Mr. Babic began to exhibit turned into a dangerous game, a dangerous game without an end, and what was it all about? Professor Raskovic wasn't interested in power; he wanted to serve his people, which was in direct opposition to Mr. Babic. Mr. Raskovic and all his intellectual abilities which were above average, he put all of this at the service of the people, while Mr. Babic put all his facilities into obtaining power. Mr. Babic was a lot more radical and he had surprising moves that surprised even Mr. Raskovic because they were contrary to his views.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you say Babic's moves were more radical. Can you tell us exactly how his radical stance manifested itself?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It manifested itself through his day-to-day statements and interviews, through the fact that he proclaimed that everything that was Croatian was Ustasha-like, through the creation of new institutions which did not bring anything positive to the people in that area; rather, the ulterior motive was personal promotion and advancement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. In paragraph 13 you say that, among other things, Babic was elected the president of the associated municipalities of Northern Dalmatia. Can you tell us who was behind the initiative to set up this association?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the result of a joint agreement really, unaware of the fact that the creation of this association of municipalities and its bodies would actually produce the opposite effect. Mr. Babic became president of the associated municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika on the 26th of June, 1990. Together with his team, Risto Matkovic and others, his close associates, he participated in the creation and setting up of the various bodies of the association of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in paragraph 14 you speak of the establishment of yet another Serbian body, namely the Serbian National Council. Why was it that after the association of municipalities was set up another body was created which related to the same people, to the same area, and had a similar purpose?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as I said a moment ago, Professor Raskovic told to Mr. Tudjman that they would respond to a move with another move just like in a game of chess. By that point, the Republic of Croatia has indicated clearly that -- its intention to settle scores with the Serb people and posed a threat to them. The Serb people, fearful of the situation because of the difficult past experience, sought to protect themselves. And the only project where the late Professor Raskovic did not take part was the creation on the 25th of July of that particular council in Srb. And it was in fact a fait accompli that the Serbian National Council was set up, and it was only natural that Milan Babic would be elected its president. Let me note that before the 25th of July Professor Raskovic endured terrible -- a terrible humiliation. I stayed behind in Srb to wait for him and he went to Zagreb for a 25-minute meeting with President Franjo Tudjman, who presented him with that notorious phonogram and tried to compromise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. There was a great deal of discussion yesterday about the arming of the reserve police force and so on. I'm putting to you a general question. Do you recall in the SFRY in general terms before the outbreak of hostilities if the police stations did have weapons in stock for their reserve force? And if so, do you know where the weapons were stored?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Police stations did have their armaments which were kept, as far as I know, in storage facilities that were part of -- part of the police station compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what sort of weapons were these? Long-barrelled, short-barrelled, automatic, semi-automatic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were short-barrelled, automatic, and semi-automatic weapons, including ammunition of course. These were rifles, pistols, semi-automatic rifles, automatic rifles, and I think they were -- or, rather, I do know that this is the sort of weapons that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, in August of 1990, the Croatian police and Croatian forces tried in these municipalities of Knin, Benkovac, and Obrovac to take out the weapons belonging to the reserve police force from the warehouses where they were kept; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And is it also not true that in this attempt to -- that in fact it was a failed attempt on their part to take the weapons kept in these reserve police warehouses; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the weapons belonging to the reserve police force in the municipalities of Northern Dalmatia remained in the locations where they always were, namely the warehouses belonging to police stations; right?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in paragraph 19 of your statement you say that barricades were erected along the roads in Northern Dalmatia, and we're talking about the August of 1990. This is my question: Do you know if the population had been mobilised to man these barricades or did they come to be there in some other way?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a state of war was declared, and in view of the fact that there was a daily threat from an imminent raid by the Croatian police forces, people spontaneously erected these barricades. I'm convinced that the barricades were not the result of an organised action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you did mention it before but I'd like to clarify one issue. Do you know if in Knin and the general surroundings there was a unit of the Yugoslav People's Army deployed?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Knin was a large centre of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, which units were deployed in and around Knin and, if you know, how many barracks were there in the town and in its immediate surroundings?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town of Knin and its immediate surroundings, there were large barracks. There was a command post in town, there was Slavko Rodic barracks, there was Juzni Logor barracks, as well as forward posts, because the -- a call was stationed there. They had their forward command posts in Dosnica, which in fact is near Golubic, so you might say that it was also called Golubic, although we referred to it as Dosnica. They had their post in Strmica, Trbonj [phoen]. Benkovac came under the Knin corps as well. And they had a number of military installations, other military installations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel turn his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the Knin Corps had its warehouses, weapons, and materiel and technical equipment? And if so, where were these warehouses located?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that they had their warehouses holding materiel and technical equipment in the -- within the perimeter of the barracks. They had huge warehouses in Dosnica as well as huge warehouses in Trbonj, near Benkovac. So they had a number of warehouses for materiel and technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned the warehouse in Dosnica. It's also referred to as Golubic, is it not, because it's close to Golubic; right?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's some 4 to 5 kilometres away from Golubic, because Golubic is the sort of location that stretches across several kilometres, and from the edge of Golubic you could say that it is 4 to 5 kilometres to Dosnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was a huge warehouse in Dosnica. Can you tell us, what did you mean precisely by that?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former system, this warehouse was housing reserves of materiel and technical equipment, assets, and weapons for the needs of the entire general area. When I say huge, I mean to say that it held mortars, shells, rockets, rifles, machine-guns. It was planned to house assets for the entire Dalmatia, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximation of the quantity? Was it measurable in tonnes, dozens of tonnes? Can you give us some sort of an idea?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you could measure it in thousands of tonnes rather than tens of tonnes. It was a huge underground storage facility located deep inside a hill. I myself never went there, but I was told about it by individuals. Access was not allowed to civilians. This was off limits to them. And only those who were working for the JNA were able to gain access to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know if the weapons of the Territorial Defence were also housed in that warehouse or one of the warehouses you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know but I believe that the weapons of the Territorial Defence were not housed in these warehouses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, may I take it that you considered the size and the dimension of the storage relevant because it may have included TO equipment as well; is that how I have to understand your line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I'm interested in knowing the quantity of weapons present in the Knin area and their whereabouts. And in passing I just wanted to ask if the TO weapons were stored there as well, but it's not central to my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the storage of JNA weapons in general, what's the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my understanding is that one of the counts of the indictment against my client is the arming of the general area. Therefore, I want to demonstrate what the quantity of weapons present in the area was. That's the purpose behind my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if I understand matters well, then the central issue therefore is whether the weapons available, whether they were used, or whether the Prosecution is right in claiming that weapons were brought from somewhere else and that -- so therefore the first and the -- I would say the most important question is how these weapons stored were used or made available to relevant parties, isn't it? If you start with that question, then we either get a confirmation that they were delivered or distributed or whatever way. And then, of course, it's important to know the details. I do not know what the answer of the witness would be and whether he has any knowledge about it because that is, I would say, decisive for the relevance of going into the details. What was there, where it was, et cetera, and that becomes relevant once you have put some other questions to the witness, which, I would say, are the -- as far as I can see, are the most important ones at the moment. Could you please come to the point as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. Thank you, Your Honour. I put the question in the context of not only this witness's testimony, but in the context of the testimony of the witnesses to come. And that then may be helpful to the Chamber. But I will not be dwelling on this point because the witness did make a couple of statements on this issue, so I will move on. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in your statement in paragraph 20 you say that Babic informed people in general on the 17th of August that a state of war had been declared. You go on to say that the weapons were taken to Golubic and taken by those who needed them. Do you know why Golubic was the place to go to on the 17th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of August, 1990, the intention was to have people go because there were stories circulating that people had set off from Gracac, that people had set off from Drnis. And since everybody was panic-stricken, it was impossible to distribute weapons in the centre of town. My understanding was that this was the reason why Golubic was chosen, as an isolated area, a youth resort which had not been under anybody's control, and most importantly to have some control over the distribution of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who Dragan Karna is?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Karna is a former inspector who used to work in Sinj. Following the impending clashes in Croatia, he left Sinj and with his family moved to Knin. And otherwise he does hail from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if Dragan Karna was engaged in a unit at that time in 1990 in the territory of Knin?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember the exact date but a so-called Special Police Unit was formed and Dragan Karna became its commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you don't recall the date, but can you tell us the year or the time of year when the unit was formed?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this unit was formed either in December or possibly in January, but it was around that time. It was in that two-month period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please tell us who composed this unit that was commanded by Dragan Karna.

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit was composed of local people, either from the active or the reserve force, but those who had the best mental and physical abilities, those who were the most capable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, where was this unit accommodated? Where was it based?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it didn't go to the field, this unit carried out tasks in the Knin SUP, but otherwise the unit was accommodated in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how many members were there in Dragan Karna's special unit?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Karna's Special Police Unit, I can't be precise about the number but I think there were between one to two platoons, meaning between 30 to 60 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And one more thing: When you say in Golubic, which facilities are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the same facilities that we discussed before that were being renovated, the school centre in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. In paragraph 37 of your statement, you spoke about the quarrel between Captain Dragan and Milan Babic about hoisting the flag on the Knin fortress. You said that this was on the 2nd of August, 1991. Can you tell us how you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a big religious holiday which is marked in the area. It's the day of St. Ilija. Milan Babic sent one of his followers, Djoko Majstorovic, to hoist the flag of the Territorial Defence on the fortress. We heard that Captain Dragan prevented it from happening and that after this there were some big quarrels between Milan Babic and Captain Dragan. I'm deeply convinced that this quarrel was in the making a long time before, because the hoisting of the flag itself was just there in order to provoke a quarrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After the quarrel of 2nd of August, what happened to Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that quarrel, Captain Dragan left Knin and the Krajina and as far as I knew he went to Belgrade. However - and it's very important to mention this - two or three days before or two or three days after, Mr. Babic staged an assassination attempt on his life which of course didn't happen. Branko Mirkovic who was at his house at the time said that his best man --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we heard that yesterday. Thank you, it's in your statement. Tell us briefly, if you know, which flag did this man want to hoist on the fortress and what flag was there before? Which flag did he want to remove and which flag did he want to put up?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before then I believe it was the regular Serbian flag. And believe me that the flag of the Territorial Defence, I never saw it myself so I can't really describe to you what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. And finally, the next arrival of Captain Dragan in Krajina is connected to 1993 and Bruska?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I recall, there was an attack on the Zadar hinterland at the time. The attack happened on the 21st of February, 1993, and I personally met with Martic at the time, who told me that Captain Dragan had arrived. I wanted to cancel hospitality but I felt sorry for him, he came with three or four people. I'm not sure whether he can help me, but I felt uncomfortable telling him to go. And when Dragan came in 1993, he set up another camp in Bruska that I never visited. And he also set up a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well, witness. Please tell us whether you know who Dusan Bandic is.

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I don't know, but I read in the papers that Dusan Bandic, Dusan Saric, a man called Stefanovic, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, were arrested in Dvor Na Uni in November of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, had any contacts with Milan Babic in that time-period that you're talking about in late 1990?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know personally. But Nebojsa Mandinic told me that they met, that is, Milan Babic and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, I guess in

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: think he was here, I think Milan Babic was here with some men and that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was among them. As for whether that is true, I don't know, but I believe my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to show you a document. It's 2D535.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have it on the screen. I would like the witness to look at paragraph 1 of the document. Could we zoom in so the witness could read it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the first paragraph. Read it and then I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, does what is in the first paragraph correspond more or less to what you know about Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know the Simatovic Defence is in the course of trying to acquire original documents. I do not know if this is one of them. We would just ask that it remain marked for identification until the original is received.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you apparently are silent on the matter. Madam Registrar, the MFI number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D332, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D332 is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also notice that you've taken approximately your 45 minutes, but if you need a few more minutes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll be done within three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you mentioned Babic's constant attempts to form some kind of an army of his own. I would like you to look at a document, P1999. Paragraph 1 of the document. Please tell us whether you know anything about the event described in this document.

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this document. I don't know anything about the document as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you about the event. Do you know anything about the event?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the event that is described here?

utterances.speaker: DST-043 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that event. On that occasion an army was formed, without an army. I would say that this was one of the political magician tricks, and I believe Rade Cubrilo was appointed commander of the army. Petar Mirkonjic was in charge of the regiment. Rajko Ilic was in charge of logistics, and so on. This was one of those desperate attempts that lasted throughout the war in Krajina. It was a desperate attempt to seize the army, the police, civilian authorities, and it was completely out of place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Weber, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just one housekeeping matter. The Prosecution was just checking and D332 that was just marked for identification which came from a published book from the Croatian authorities, we were just comparing it to D98 which appears to be already an exhibit, and we believe that these may be the same documents. If Mr. Petrovic wishes to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, if you would please check that. And if it is -- if Mr. Weber is right, perhaps the MFI number could be vacated soon. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
